days.title: Cloud Computing, Shared Responsibility, and Cloud Models

concepts.heading: What Cloud Computing Is
concepts.body: Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services, such as virtual machines, storage, databases, networking and analytics, over the internet. Instead of buying and racking your own servers, you rent capacity from a provider like Microsoft and use it as long as you need it. Because the provider has already built the datacenters, you can create a new server in minutes and delete it when the work is finished, and you never have to plan a hardware refresh. For example, a small design studio that needs extra rendering power for one month can create virtual machines in Azure for that month only, instead of buying workstations that would sit idle afterwards. On the exam, cloud computing is described as renting compute, storage and networking on demand over the internet, with the provider owning and running the physical infrastructure.

concepts.heading: The Shared Responsibility Model
concepts.body: In a traditional datacenter the company is responsible for everything, from the building and power to the applications and data. In the cloud, responsibility is shared between Microsoft and the customer. Microsoft is always responsible for the physical datacenter, the physical network and the physical hosts. The customer is always responsible for the information and data stored in the cloud, the devices allowed to connect, and the accounts and identities of its people. Everything in between, such as the operating system, network controls and applications, moves between the two depending on the service type. With an Azure virtual machine (IaaS) the customer patches the operating system; with a SaaS product such as Microsoft 365 Microsoft runs nearly everything. A question that asks who classifies data or protects user accounts always answers the customer, whatever the service type.

concepts.heading: Public, Private, and Hybrid Clouds
concepts.body: A private cloud is used by a single organization, usually in its own datacenter or in a dedicated hosted facility, so it gives full control but requires buying and maintaining the hardware. A public cloud is built, controlled and maintained by a third-party provider such as Azure, and anyone can buy services from it; there is no up-front hardware cost and you can scale quickly, but you do not control the physical hardware. A hybrid cloud connects a private cloud and a public cloud so that workloads and data can move between them. For example, a hospital might keep a patient records system on premises for regulatory reasons while running its public appointment website and backups in Azure, with the two connected. If a scenario keeps some systems on site and uses Azure for others, connected together, the answer is hybrid.

concepts.heading: Multicloud and Azure Arc
concepts.body: Multicloud means using two or more public cloud providers at the same time, for example running a data platform in Azure while a marketing site stays with another provider. Organizations choose multicloud to use the best service from each provider or because of acquisitions, but it means working with several management tools and billing systems. Azure Arc helps with that problem: it extends Azure management to servers, Kubernetes clusters and data services that run outside Azure, whether on premises or in another cloud. Once connected, those machines appear in Azure and can be organized with resource groups and tags, governed with Azure Policy and secured with Azure tools. Arc does not move the workload into Azure or give it Azure capacity. When a question asks how to manage on-premises or other-cloud servers from Azure in one place, choose Azure Arc.

concepts.heading: Azure VMware Solution
concepts.body: Many companies run their servers on VMware vSphere in their own datacenter. Azure VMware Solution lets them run those VMware workloads in Azure without converting the virtual machines. It provides private clouds built from dedicated bare-metal Azure hosts that run the VMware stack, including vSphere, vCenter Server and vSAN, so administrators keep using the VMware tools and skills they already have. A typical example is a company whose datacenter lease is ending: it moves its VMware virtual machines into Azure VMware Solution, keeps its vCenter-based processes, and can then connect them to native Azure services over time. Compare it with Azure Arc, which manages servers that stay outside Azure, and with Azure Migrate, which moves servers into standard Azure virtual machines. If the scenario stresses keeping VMware tools and moving VMware workloads to Azure, the answer is Azure VMware Solution.

examPoints: A question that asks who is responsible for data, devices, or user accounts and identities in the cloud is testing the shared responsibility model: the customer always keeps these, while Microsoft always owns the physical datacenter, network, and hosts.
A question that describes some systems kept on premises and others in Azure, connected together, is testing hybrid cloud; one that describes two or more public providers is testing multicloud.

A question that asks how to manage servers outside Azure from the Azure portal is testing Azure Arc, while one about moving VMware workloads to Azure while keeping VMware tools is testing Azure VMware Solution.

quiz.q: A company runs a web app on Azure virtual machines. Which task remains the company's responsibility under the shared responsibility model?
choices: Replacing failed disks in the physical servers that host the virtual machines
Securing the physical network cabling inside the Azure datacenter building
Managing the user accounts and identities that sign in to the application
Providing backup power and cooling for the racks that hold the hosts
quiz.explain: The customer always keeps responsibility for accounts and identities, whatever the service type. Choice A is tempting because disks hold the customer's data, but physical hardware in the datacenter is always Microsoft's job.

quiz.q: A retailer keeps its stock database in its own datacenter and runs servers in Azure and in another public cloud. It wants to tag, govern and monitor all of these servers from one place in Azure. What should it use?
choices: Azure Arc, connecting the on-premises and other-cloud servers to Azure management
Azure VMware Solution, running every server on dedicated VMware hosts in Azure
A private cloud, rebuilding all servers on hardware in the retailer's datacenter
Azure Migrate, assessing every server and moving it into Azure virtual machines
quiz.explain: Azure Arc projects servers that stay outside Azure into Azure management so they can be tagged, governed and monitored. Choice D is tempting, but Azure Migrate moves servers into Azure, and the retailer wants to keep them where they are.

days.recap: Cloud computing rents compute, storage and networking on demand under a shared responsibility model, and it can be deployed as public, private, hybrid or multicloud, with Azure Arc managing resources outside Azure and Azure VMware Solution hosting VMware workloads in Azure.

days.title: Consumption-Based Model, Pricing Options, and Serverless

concepts.heading: CapEx, OpEx, and the Consumption-Based Model
concepts.body: Capital expenditure (CapEx) is a one-time, up-front spend on physical things such as servers and buildings, whose value is used up over years. Operational expenditure (OpEx) is spending on services or products over time, such as a monthly bill. Cloud computing is OpEx: you rent capacity and pay for what you use. This is the consumption-based model. You do not pay up front, you do not have to buy and manage expensive infrastructure, you can pay for extra resources when you need them, and you stop paying for resources you no longer need. For example, a tax firm can run extra virtual machines in the busy months before the filing deadline and delete them afterwards, paying only for the weeks they ran. On the exam, no up-front cost and paying only for what you use point to the consumption-based model and OpEx.

concepts.heading: Pay-as-You-Go and Commitment Discounts
concepts.body: Pay-as-you-go is the default way to pay for Azure: you are billed for the resources you use, with no commitment, so it suits short, new or unpredictable workloads. When usage is steady, two commitment options lower the price. Azure Reservations commit you to a specific resource, such as a virtual machine size in a region, for one or three years, which fits a database server that has run on the same size for years. An Azure savings plan for compute commits you to an hourly spend amount on eligible compute services for one or three years, and the discount follows your usage across sizes, services and regions, which fits workloads that keep changing shape. Both are billing discounts only; they do not change how the resource runs. Stable size and region suggests a reservation; steady spend with changing services or regions suggests a savings plan.

concepts.heading: Spot Virtual Machines
concepts.body: Azure Spot Virtual Machines let you use Azure's unused compute capacity at a large discount compared with pay-as-you-go. The trade-off is that Azure can evict a Spot VM whenever it needs the capacity back, and Spot VMs have no SLA. That makes them a poor choice for production web servers or databases, but a good fit for work that can be stopped and restarted, such as batch processing jobs, rendering, large calculations that save progress as they go, or dev and test environments. For example, a research team that processes images overnight can run the job on Spot VMs and simply resume any part that was interrupted. Remember that eviction is not a failure on Microsoft's part; it is the deal you accepted for the lower price. If a scenario stresses lowest cost for interruptible work, choose Spot; if it stresses uptime, avoid Spot.

concepts.heading: Azure Hybrid Benefit
concepts.body: Azure Hybrid Benefit lets you use licenses you already own to lower the cost of running workloads in Azure. It is best known for Windows Server and SQL Server licenses covered by active Software Assurance or qualifying subscription licenses, and it also covers Red Hat Enterprise Linux and SUSE Linux Enterprise subscriptions. Instead of paying again for the Windows Server or SQL Server license as part of the Azure price, you pay a reduced rate, usually closer to the base compute cost. For example, a company that moves its on-premises Windows servers to Azure virtual machines can turn on Azure Hybrid Benefit for them and avoid paying twice for licenses it already holds. Hybrid Benefit is about software licensing, while reservations and savings plans discount the compute itself, so a company can combine them. A question that mentions existing Windows Server or SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance is pointing to Azure Hybrid Benefit.

concepts.heading: Serverless Computing
concepts.body: Serverless does not mean there are no servers. It means the cloud provider runs and scales the servers for you, so you never provision, patch or size them. Serverless services are usually event-driven, they scale automatically, including down to nothing when idle, and on consumption-style plans you pay for the time your code actually runs rather than for idle servers. Azure Functions is the classic example: a small piece of code runs when something happens, such as a file arriving in storage, a message on a queue, an HTTP request or a timer. For example, a photo site can run a function that creates a thumbnail each time a user uploads an image, and it costs almost nothing at night when nobody uploads. On the exam, short event-triggered tasks with unpredictable demand and no wish to manage servers point to serverless and Azure Functions.

examPoints: A question that contrasts buying hardware up front with paying a monthly bill for what is used is testing CapEx versus OpEx and the consumption-based model.

A question about a steady workload on a fixed VM size and region is testing reservations, one about steady spend that moves across services and regions is testing a savings plan, and one about cheap interruptible batch work is testing Spot Virtual Machines.
A question that mentions existing Windows Server or SQL Server licenses is testing Azure Hybrid Benefit, while one about code that runs only when an event happens is testing serverless computing.

quiz.q: A company has run the same VM size in the same region for three years and expects that to continue. It wants the lowest compute price for that VM. Which option fits best?
choices: Azure Spot Virtual Machines, which use spare capacity that Azure can reclaim
Pay-as-you-go pricing, which bills each hour of use with no commitment at all
Azure Hybrid Benefit, which reuses existing Windows Server and SQL Server licenses
An Azure reservation, which commits to that VM size and region for one or three years
quiz.explain: A stable, specific size and region is the textbook case for a reservation. Choice A is tempting because Spot is cheap, but Spot VMs can be evicted and have no SLA, which does not suit a long-running production server.

quiz.q: Each time a scanned invoice lands in a storage account, a small script must extract its total. Invoices arrive at random times, and the team does not want to manage servers. What should it use?
choices: A virtual machine scale set that keeps two Windows servers running at all times
Azure Functions, running the script when each new file arrives in storage
An Azure reservation for a virtual machine that runs the script on a schedule
Azure VMware Solution, hosting the script on dedicated vSphere hosts in Azure
quiz.explain: A function triggered by the new file runs only when needed and needs no server management, which is serverless. Choice A is tempting because scale sets automate capacity, but the servers run and cost money all the time and must still be managed.

days.recap: Azure uses an OpEx, consumption-based model: pay-as-you-go by default, reservations or savings plans for steady usage, Spot VMs for interruptible work, Azure Hybrid Benefit for existing licenses, and serverless services such as Azure Functions to pay only when code runs.

days.title: Benefits of the Cloud and IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS

concepts.heading: High Availability and Scalability
concepts.body: High availability means an application stays up and reachable even when individual components fail, usually because there are redundant copies of it spread across hardware or locations. Azure describes its availability commitments in service-level agreements (SLAs), formal documents that state what Microsoft commits to for each service and what credit you receive if it falls short. Running more than one instance, for example across availability zones, can qualify for a stronger SLA, while preview features and Spot VMs have no SLA. Scalability is the ability to adjust resources to meet demand. Vertical scaling (scaling up or down) changes the size of a resource, such as giving a VM more CPUs; horizontal scaling (scaling out or in) changes the number of instances. Elasticity is scaling that happens automatically. A shop that adds web servers during a sale and removes them afterwards is using horizontal, elastic scaling.

concepts.heading: Reliability and Predictability
concepts.body: Reliability is the ability of a system to recover from failures and keep functioning. The cloud supports it through its decentralized design: you can deploy resources in regions around the world, so even a regional disaster does not have to take down every copy of your application if you designed for it. Predictability comes in two forms. Performance predictability means you can count on the resources you need to serve customers, using features such as autoscaling and load balancing. Cost predictability means you can forecast spending, using tools such as the pricing calculator, Microsoft Cost Management and budgets, and real-time tracking of usage. The Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework gives guidance for both. On the exam, recovering from failures maps to reliability, while knowing what performance you will get or what you will pay maps to predictability.

concepts.heading: Security, Governance, and Manageability
concepts.body: The cloud helps with security and governance because you can deploy from templates that already meet company standards and use cloud-based auditing to flag resources that drift from those standards. With PaaS and SaaS, patches and maintenance can be taken care of for you, and cloud providers are well suited to handling threats such as distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks. Manageability has two sides. Management of the cloud means managing the resources themselves: scaling automatically, deploying from templates, monitoring health and replacing failing resources, and getting alerts. Management in the cloud means the ways you can manage it: through the web-based Azure portal, a command-line interface, APIs, or PowerShell. For example, a bank that wants every new storage account to meet its rules can deploy from a standard template and audit for exceptions. Questions about meeting standards point to governance; questions about tools and automation point to manageability.

concepts.heading: IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS
concepts.body: Infrastructure as a service (IaaS) gives you the most control and the most responsibility: the provider keeps the physical hardware, network and datacenter running, and you manage the operating system, configuration, patching and applications. Azure Virtual Machines is the classic example, used for lift-and-shift migration and for testing and development. Platform as a service (PaaS) sits in the middle: Microsoft manages the hardware and the operating system, so you focus on your application and data; Azure App Service and Azure SQL Database are examples. Software as a service (SaaS) is a complete application that you simply use, such as Microsoft 365 for email and documents; you manage the data, devices and user access. Moving from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS, you manage less and control less. This ladder ties directly to the shared responsibility model you learned on day 1.

concepts.heading: Choosing a Service Type by Use Case
concepts.body: Exam questions often describe a need and ask which service type fits. Pick IaaS when you need full control of the operating system or must move existing servers with few changes, for example an old application that needs a specific OS setting, or a lift-and-shift migration. Pick PaaS when a development team wants to deploy its own code without patching servers and wants built-in scaling and availability, for example a team that publishes a web API to Azure App Service from its Git repository. Pick SaaS when users just need a finished application, such as email, calendars, office documents or a customer relationship management tool, and nobody wants to build or run software. A useful test is to ask what the customer still manages: everything above the hardware is IaaS, only the code and data is PaaS, and only data and access is SaaS.

examPoints: A question that describes adding instances is testing horizontal scaling, one that describes making a single resource bigger is testing vertical scaling, and one about staying up when components fail is testing high availability.

A question about deploying from standard templates and auditing for drift is testing the security and governance benefit, while one about portal, CLI, API, or PowerShell access is testing manageability.
A question that asks who patches the operating system is testing IaaS versus PaaS: the customer patches it on IaaS, Microsoft patches it on PaaS and SaaS.

quiz.q: A team wants to publish its own web application without patching or managing any operating system, and it wants built-in scaling. Which service type fits best?
choices: Infrastructure as a service, using Azure virtual machines the team configures itself
Software as a service, subscribing to a finished application such as Microsoft 365
Platform as a service, deploying the code to a managed service such as Azure App Service
A private cloud, running the application on servers in the company's own datacenter
quiz.explain: PaaS lets the team deploy its own code while Microsoft manages the operating system and provides scaling. Choice B is tempting because SaaS also removes OS work, but SaaS is a finished product, so the team could not run its own application on it.

quiz.q: During a monthly report run, an administrator moves a database VM to a size with more CPUs and memory, then back afterwards. What is this an example of?
choices: Vertical scaling, changing the size of a single resource up and then down
Horizontal scaling, adding more instances of the database and removing them later
High availability, keeping the database running when a physical host fails
Reliability, recovering the database in another region after a regional disaster
quiz.explain: Changing the size of one resource is vertical scaling. Choice B is tempting because capacity also increases, but horizontal scaling changes the number of instances, not the size of one.

days.recap: The cloud brings high availability and scalability, reliability and predictability, security and governance, and manageability, delivered as IaaS, PaaS or SaaS according to how much of the stack you want to manage yourself.

days.title: Core Architecture: Regions, Zones, and the Resource Hierarchy

concepts.heading: Regions, Datacenters, and Region Pairs
concepts.body: Azure datacenters are facilities with racks of servers, power, cooling and networking. They are not used directly; they are grouped into regions. A region is a geographical area containing at least one, and often several, nearby datacenters connected by a low-latency network. You choose a region when you create most resources, usually close to your users or where data must legally stay, and not every service or VM size is offered in every region. Microsoft associates some regions with another region in the same geography, usually hundreds of miles away, to form a region pair. A few services use the pair, for example geo-redundant storage replicates to the paired region, and Microsoft staggers planned updates across a pair. Pairing alone does not give your application failover: you must deploy to the second region and plan recovery yourself. Many newer regions are nonpaired and rely on availability zones.

concepts.heading: Availability Zones
concepts.body: An availability zone is a physically separate group of one or more datacenters inside an Azure region, with independent power, cooling and networking. Zones are close enough to be connected by a high-speed, low-latency network but far enough apart that a local problem such as a fire or power cut in one zone should not affect the others. Regions that support zones have at least three of them, although not every region supports zones. You use them in two ways: zonal services, such as a VM pinned to one zone, and zone-redundant services, such as zone-redundant storage, which Azure spreads across zones for you. For example, placing two web VMs in different zones behind a load balancer keeps the site running if one datacenter fails. Match the failure to the tool: a rack failure calls for an availability set, a datacenter failure for zones, and a regional failure for a second region.

concepts.heading: Sovereign Regions
concepts.body: Most Azure regions belong to the main global Azure cloud. Sovereign regions are separate instances of Azure, isolated from that main instance, used for compliance or legal reasons. Azure Government provides physically and logically network-isolated regions in the United States for U.S. government agencies and their partners, operated by screened U.S. personnel. Azure in China is operated by 21Vianet, a separate company, rather than directly by Microsoft, and it is the way to host in mainland China, where global Azure has no regions. These clouds have their own portals and may not offer every service the global cloud has. For example, a U.S. federal agency with strict requirements would deploy to Azure Government regions such as US Gov Virginia rather than East US. When a question mentions U.S. government compliance or hosting in mainland China, the answer is a sovereign region, not a normal region pair.

concepts.heading: Resources, Resource Groups, and Subscriptions
concepts.body: A resource is any item you create in Azure, such as a virtual machine, a virtual network or a storage account. Every resource must belong to exactly one resource group, which is a logical container for resources that share a lifecycle. Deleting a resource group deletes everything in it, and settings such as role assignments applied to a resource group are inherited by the resources inside. Resource groups cannot be nested, and the resources inside one can be in different regions. A resource group in turn belongs to one subscription. A subscription is a unit of management, billing and scale: it is linked to one Azure account, and separate subscriptions are often used to split environments such as development and production, or to give each department its own bill and access limits. For example, a team can put all the resources of a test project in one resource group and delete them together.

concepts.heading: Management Groups and the Hierarchy
concepts.body: When an organization has many subscriptions, management groups organize them. A management group can contain subscriptions and other management groups, forming a tree under a single root management group, up to six levels deep below the root. Azure Policy assignments and role-based access control assignments made at a management group are inherited by every subscription, resource group and resource below it, so one rule can cover hundreds of subscriptions. Each subscription and management group has only one parent. The full hierarchy, from broadest to narrowest, is management groups, subscriptions, resource groups and resources, and Azure Resource Manager is the deployment and management service that applies settings at each level. For example, a company can create a Production management group, assign a policy that allows only European regions, and every production subscription under it inherits that restriction. Questions about applying one rule to many subscriptions point to management groups.

examPoints: A question that asks how to survive the failure of one datacenter inside a region is testing availability zones; one that assumes a region pair fails over automatically is testing whether you know pairing alone does not provide failover.
A question about U.S. government compliance or hosting in mainland China is testing sovereign regions such as Azure Government and Azure operated by 21Vianet.

A question about applying one policy or role assignment to many subscriptions is testing management groups and inheritance down the hierarchy of management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, and resources.

quiz.q: A company has 40 subscriptions and wants a single Azure Policy assignment to apply to all of them, including subscriptions created later in the same structure. Where should it assign the policy?
choices: On each resource group, so that every workload receives its own copy of the rule
On a management group that contains all the subscriptions in the organization
On one subscription, which then shares its policies with the other subscriptions
On a region pair, so that both regions enforce the policy for every subscription
quiz.explain: Assignments on a management group are inherited by every subscription beneath it. Choice C is tempting, but settings on one subscription flow down to its own resource groups, never across to sibling subscriptions.

quiz.q: An online store runs two VMs in one Azure region and wants the site to survive the loss of an entire datacenter in that region. What should it do?
choices: Rely on the region pair, which moves the VMs to the paired region automatically
Place both VMs in the same resource group so Azure can restart them together
Deploy the VMs to a sovereign region, which uses separate isolated datacenters
Place the VMs in different availability zones behind a load balancer in that region
quiz.explain: Availability zones are separate datacenter groups inside a region, so spreading VMs across them survives a datacenter failure. Choice A is tempting, but a region pair does not move workloads by itself; you must deploy and fail over to the second region yourself.

days.recap: Azure's physical layers are datacenters, availability zones, regions, region pairs and sovereign regions, and its management layers are resources, resource groups, subscriptions and management groups, with settings inherited down that hierarchy.

days.title: Compute: Virtual Machines, Containers, Functions, and App Service

concepts.heading: Virtual Machines and What They Need
concepts.body: Azure Virtual Machines are IaaS: you get a virtualized server with full control of the operating system and the software on it, without buying hardware. They suit lift-and-shift migrations, applications that need a specific OS setting, and test environments. When you create a VM you make several choices: the operating system image (Windows or Linux, or a Marketplace image with software preinstalled), the size (the number of CPUs and the memory, grouped into families such as general purpose or memory optimized), the disks for the OS and data, and networking, meaning a virtual network, a network interface and optionally a public IP address. The VM belongs to a resource group and region like any resource. Because it is IaaS, you patch and configure the operating system yourself. For example, a company moving a legacy accounting server would pick a matching OS image and a size close to its current server.

concepts.heading: Availability Sets and Virtual Machine Scale Sets
concepts.body: An availability set groups VMs that you create so that Azure spreads them across fault domains, which share power and network hardware, and update domains, which are rebooted at different times during planned maintenance. It costs nothing extra beyond the VMs and protects against a rack or host failure, but it does not add or remove VMs. Virtual Machine Scale Sets manage a group of identical, load-balanced VMs and can increase or decrease the number of instances automatically based on demand or a schedule, which makes them the IaaS answer for elastic web tiers. For example, a news site expects heavy traffic during an election night: a scale set adds VMs as CPU load rises and removes them afterwards. On the exam, a fixed group of VMs that must survive hardware failure points to availability sets, while identical VMs that grow and shrink automatically point to scale sets.

concepts.heading: Azure Virtual Desktop
concepts.body: Azure Virtual Desktop is a desktop and app virtualization service that runs on Azure. Users connect from almost any device, including a web browser, to a full Windows desktop or to individual applications that run in Azure, so the company's data stays in Azure rather than on the user's laptop. Administrators manage the desktops centrally, and Azure Virtual Desktop supports multi-session editions such as Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session, which let several users share one session host VM to lower cost. It integrates with Microsoft Entra ID for sign-in and with security features such as multifactor authentication. A typical scenario is a company that hires contractors who use their own devices: giving them Azure Virtual Desktop sessions lets them work with company apps without copying data to personal machines. If a question describes remote users needing a managed Windows desktop from any device, the answer is Azure Virtual Desktop.

concepts.heading: Containers: ACI, Container Apps, and AKS
concepts.body: A container packages an application with its dependencies, so it runs the same way everywhere, and it starts much faster than a VM because it does not boot a full operating system. Azure offers three main ways to run them. Azure Container Instances is the simplest: you run a single container or small group of containers on demand without managing servers, which suits quick tasks and simple apps. Azure Container Apps is a serverless platform for microservices and container jobs, with built-in load balancing, autoscaling (including scale to zero) and revisions, without direct access to Kubernetes APIs. Azure Kubernetes Service is a managed Kubernetes service for orchestrating large fleets of containers when you need full Kubernetes control and tools. For example, a team with one container that converts files runs it in Container Instances, while a company with dozens of microservices and Kubernetes skills chooses AKS.

concepts.heading: Azure Functions and App Service
concepts.body: Azure Functions is the serverless compute option: code runs in response to an event, such as an HTTP request, a timer, a new queue message or a new blob, and on a consumption-style plan it scales automatically and you pay only while the code runs. Functions are stateless by default, and Durable Functions add state for longer workflows. Azure App Service is a PaaS for hosting web-oriented applications on Windows or Linux without managing servers. It supports several app styles on the same platform: web apps, API apps, WebJobs that run background scripts, and mobile app back ends. App Service provides deployment from source control, autoscaling, and load balancing, and you choose an App Service plan that defines the compute it runs on. Choose Functions for short event-driven tasks with irregular demand, and App Service for an always-available website or API that a team deploys and updates regularly.

examPoints: A question that asks for VMs that increase and decrease in number automatically with demand is testing Virtual Machine Scale Sets, while one about protecting a fixed set of VMs from rack or maintenance outages is testing availability sets.

A question that compares container options is testing whether you match a simple single container to Azure Container Instances, serverless microservices to Azure Container Apps, and full Kubernetes orchestration to Azure Kubernetes Service.

A question about remote users needing a centrally managed Windows desktop from any device is testing Azure Virtual Desktop, and one about event-triggered code with no servers is testing Azure Functions.

quiz.q: A development team has dozens of microservices, already uses Kubernetes tools, and needs direct access to the Kubernetes API. Which Azure service fits best?
choices: Azure Container Instances, which runs single containers on demand without servers
Azure Container Apps, which runs serverless microservices with automatic scaling
Azure Functions, which runs event-triggered code on a consumption-style plan
Azure Kubernetes Service, which provides managed Kubernetes orchestration for containers
quiz.explain: AKS is managed Kubernetes with direct access to the Kubernetes API for large container fleets. Choice B is tempting because Container Apps also runs microservices, but it does not provide direct access to the Kubernetes APIs.

quiz.q: A company hires temporary staff who work on their own laptops. It wants them to use company Windows applications without storing company data on those laptops. What should it use?
choices: Azure Virtual Desktop, giving each person a managed desktop session running in Azure
Azure App Service, hosting each Windows application as a web app on a shared plan
Virtual Machine Scale Sets, adding one VM per staff member as each person signs in
Azure Container Instances, running each Windows application in its own container
quiz.explain: Azure Virtual Desktop delivers managed Windows desktops and apps from Azure to any device, so data stays in Azure. Choice C is tempting because scale sets add VMs automatically, but they host load-balanced workloads, not managed user desktops.

days.recap: Azure compute ranges from IaaS virtual machines (with availability sets and scale sets) and Azure Virtual Desktop, through containers on Container Instances, Container Apps or AKS, to serverless Azure Functions and the PaaS App Service.

days.title: Networking: Virtual Networks, DNS, VPN Gateway, and ExpressRoute

concepts.heading: Virtual Networks and Subnets
concepts.body: An Azure virtual network (VNet) is your own private network in Azure. It lets Azure resources such as VMs communicate with each other, with the internet, and with on-premises networks. When you create a VNet you give it a private address space, for example 10.0.0.0/16, and divide it into subnets, such as 10.0.1.0/24 for web servers and 10.0.2.0/24 for databases. Resources in the same VNet can talk to each other by default, and you control traffic with network security groups that allow or deny traffic by address, port and protocol. Internet access works both ways: resources can reach out to the internet, and you can expose a resource to inbound traffic with a public IP address or a load balancer. A VNet belongs to one region and one subscription. On the exam, isolating and segmenting Azure resources on a private network is a virtual network and subnets.

concepts.heading: Virtual Network Peering
concepts.body: Virtual network peering connects two Azure virtual networks so that resources in each can communicate as if they were on the same network. Traffic between peered networks is private: it stays on the Microsoft backbone network and never travels over the public internet. Peering works between VNets in the same region and, as global virtual network peering, between VNets in different regions, and it can connect VNets in different subscriptions. For example, a company with a shared services VNet holding domain controllers and monitoring tools in West Europe can peer it with application VNets in West Europe and East US so that all applications reach those shared services. Peering connects Azure networks to each other; it is not how you connect an office. If a question asks how two Azure VNets can communicate privately without a gateway or the internet, the answer is virtual network peering.

concepts.heading: Azure DNS
concepts.body: Azure DNS is a hosting service for DNS domains that answers name lookups using Microsoft's global network of name servers. You manage your DNS records with the same Azure credentials, role-based access control, activity logs and billing as your other Azure resources. A public DNS zone answers queries from the internet, for example mapping www.contoso.com to the public IP of a web app. A private DNS zone resolves names only inside the virtual networks you link to it, so a VM can reach db.internal.contoso.com without that name being visible on the internet. Azure DNS hosts domains; you cannot buy a domain name through Azure DNS itself, so you buy it through App Service domains or a third-party domain registrar and then delegate it to Azure DNS. DNS only translates names into addresses and carries no application traffic. A question about managing a company's DNS records in Azure alongside its other resources points to Azure DNS.

concepts.heading: VPN Gateway and ExpressRoute
concepts.body: Two services connect on-premises sites to Azure. Azure VPN Gateway sends encrypted traffic between an Azure virtual network and another location over the public internet. A site-to-site connection links an office's VPN device to the Azure gateway, so every device in that office reaches Azure. A point-to-site connection links one computer to the Azure gateway, which suits a remote worker on a laptop with no VPN hardware. VPN Gateway can also link two Azure VNets (network-to-network). Azure ExpressRoute extends an on-premises network into the Microsoft cloud over a private connection provided by a connectivity provider; the traffic does not go over the public internet, which gives more reliability, consistent latency and higher bandwidth. For example, a bank that moves large volumes of data daily and needs predictable performance chooses ExpressRoute, while a small branch office uses site-to-site VPN. Encrypted over the internet means VPN; private and not over the internet means ExpressRoute.

concepts.heading: Public and Private Endpoints
concepts.body: Many Azure PaaS services, such as Azure Storage and Azure SQL Database, are reached through a public endpoint by default. A public endpoint has a public IP address and can be accessed from anywhere on the internet, subject to the service's firewall and access rules, which is what a public website needs. A private endpoint is a network interface inside your virtual network with a private IP address from that VNet's address space. It connects privately to a specific service powered by Azure Private Link, so traffic between your VNet and the service stays on the Microsoft network. For example, a company can give its storage account a private endpoint, disable public network access, and let only VMs in its VNet and offices connected by VPN or ExpressRoute read the data. A private endpoint does not join two networks together. Private IP inside a VNet for a PaaS service means a private endpoint.

examPoints: A question that asks how two Azure virtual networks can communicate privately over the Microsoft backbone is testing virtual network peering, not VPN Gateway or ExpressRoute.

A question that compares site-to-site, point-to-site, and ExpressRoute is testing whether you know VPN Gateway encrypts traffic over the public internet, point-to-site connects one computer, and ExpressRoute uses a private connection that does not cross the internet.

A question about reaching a storage account or database through a private IP address inside a virtual network is testing private endpoints, while one about hosting DNS records with Azure access control is testing Azure DNS.

quiz.q: A consultant working from hotels needs a secure connection from her laptop to VMs in an Azure virtual network. The hotels have no VPN hardware. What should the company configure?
choices: A site-to-site VPN connection between the hotel's network device and the Azure VPN gateway
A point-to-site VPN connection that the laptop itself starts to the Azure VPN gateway
An ExpressRoute circuit from the consultant's hotel to Azure through a connectivity provider
Virtual network peering between the hotel's network and the company's Azure virtual network
quiz.explain: Point-to-site VPN connects an individual computer to the Azure gateway, with the client starting the encrypted connection. Choice A is tempting because it is also a VPN, but site-to-site needs a VPN device at the location and connects a whole network.

quiz.q: A manufacturer transfers large data volumes to Azure every day and needs consistent latency over a connection that does not travel across the public internet. What should it use?
choices: Azure VPN Gateway with a site-to-site connection that encrypts traffic over the internet
Azure DNS with a private zone that resolves the factory's servers inside the network
Azure ExpressRoute, a private connection to Microsoft through a connectivity provider
A public endpoint on each Azure service, protected by the service's own firewall rules
quiz.explain: ExpressRoute provides a private connection that does not go over the public internet, with more consistent latency and higher bandwidth. Choice A is tempting because it connects the site and encrypts data, but site-to-site VPN traffic still travels across the public internet.

days.recap: Virtual networks and subnets give Azure resources a private network, peering joins VNets privately, Azure DNS hosts public and private zones, VPN Gateway and ExpressRoute connect on-premises sites, and private endpoints bring PaaS services into a VNet.

days.title: Storage: Services, Tiers, Redundancy, and Moving Data

concepts.heading: Storage Services and Account Types
concepts.body: An Azure storage account is a container that gives your data a unique namespace reachable over HTTP or HTTPS. It offers several services. Azure Blob Storage holds unstructured data such as images, videos, backups and logs. Azure Files provides fully managed file shares reached over SMB or NFS, so many servers can mount the same share. Azure Queue Storage holds large numbers of messages that let parts of an application work asynchronously. Azure Table Storage stores structured NoSQL data as key and attribute pairs. Azure Disk Storage provides block-level volumes that Azure VMs use as disks. The recommended account type for most scenarios is standard general-purpose v2, which supports blobs, files, queues and tables. Premium account types (premium block blobs, premium file shares and premium page blobs) use solid-state drives for low latency, and each supports one kind of data. You choose the account type when you create the account, and it determines which services and redundancy options are available.

concepts.heading: Access Tiers and Lifecycle Management
concepts.body: Blob Storage offers access tiers that trade storage cost against access cost. Hot is for data accessed frequently; it has the highest storage cost and the lowest access cost. Cool is for data that is infrequently accessed and stored for at least 30 days. Cold is for data rarely accessed and stored for at least 90 days, and it is still online. Archive is for data rarely accessed and stored for at least 180 days with flexible latency; it has the lowest storage cost, but it is offline, so a blob must be rehydrated to an online tier, which can take hours, before it can be read. Archive is set per blob, never as the account default. Lifecycle management rules move or delete blobs automatically, for example moving logs to cool after 30 days, to archive after 180 days, and deleting them later. Instant access at low cost means cold; lowest cost with hours of delay means archive.

concepts.heading: Redundancy Options
concepts.body: Azure Storage always keeps multiple copies of your data. Locally redundant storage (LRS) keeps three copies within one datacenter in the primary region; it is the lowest-cost option but does not survive a datacenter-wide disaster. Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) copies data synchronously across three availability zones in the primary region, so it survives the loss of a zone. Geo-redundant storage (GRS) uses LRS in the primary region and also copies data asynchronously to a secondary region, usually the paired region. Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) combines ZRS in the primary region with a copy in a secondary region. With GRS and GZRS the secondary copy is not readable unless a failover happens; read-access versions, RA-GRS and RA-GZRS, let you read from the secondary region at any time. For example, an app that must keep serving reads during a regional outage chooses RA-GZRS. Zone loss points to ZRS; region loss points to a geo option.

concepts.heading: Moving Data: AzCopy, Storage Explorer, and File Sync
concepts.body: Several tools copy or synchronize data with Azure Storage. AzCopy is a command-line utility that copies blobs or files to, from or between storage accounts, which suits scripted and scheduled transfers; synchronization with AzCopy is one direction only. Azure Storage Explorer is a free graphical application for Windows, macOS and Linux that lets you browse, upload and download data, and it uses AzCopy underneath. Azure File Sync centralizes file shares in Azure Files while keeping Windows file servers as local caches. An agent on Windows Server keeps the server synchronized in both directions with the Azure file share, and cloud tiering can keep only frequently used files on the local disk. For example, a firm with three branch offices can use File Sync so each office has a fast local file server while one copy of the files lives in Azure. Scripted copy means AzCopy; a graphical tool means Storage Explorer; two-way file server sync means File Sync.

concepts.heading: Migration: Azure Migrate and Azure Data Box
concepts.body: Azure Migrate is a hub for moving workloads to Azure. It brings tools together in one place to discover servers (for example VMware or Hyper-V virtual machines and physical servers), assess their readiness and estimate sizes and cost in Azure, and then migrate servers, databases and web apps. Azure Data Box moves data rather than workloads. It is a physical device that you order in the Azure portal; it is delivered to your site, you copy your data onto it over the local network, and you ship it back so Microsoft uploads the data into your storage account. It is designed for very large data sets when network bandwidth is limited. For example, a film archive with a huge amount of footage and a slow internet link ships it with Data Box. Assessing and moving servers points to Azure Migrate; shipping bulk data offline points to Data Box.

examPoints: A question that asks for the cheapest tier for data that is rarely read but must open immediately is testing the cold tier, while one that accepts hours of delay is testing the archive tier and rehydration.

A question about surviving the loss of an availability zone is testing ZRS, one about surviving a regional outage is testing GRS or GZRS, and one that needs to read from the secondary region at any time is testing the read-access (RA-) versions.

A question that compares data movement tools is testing whether you match scripted copy to AzCopy, two-way sync of Windows file servers to Azure File Sync, server discovery and assessment to Azure Migrate, and offline bulk transfer to Azure Data Box.

quiz.q: A company must keep its storage account data available if one availability zone in its region fails, but it has no requirement to copy data to another region. Which redundancy option fits best?
choices: Locally redundant storage, which keeps three copies inside one datacenter in the region
Geo-redundant storage, which also copies the data asynchronously to a secondary region
Read-access geo-redundant storage, which lets apps read the secondary region at any time
Zone-redundant storage, which copies the data synchronously across three availability zones
quiz.explain: ZRS spreads copies across three availability zones in the primary region, so it survives a zone failure without a second region. Choice A is tempting because it is cheaper, but all three LRS copies sit in one datacenter, which a zone failure could take down.

quiz.q: A law firm has a huge archive of scanned files and a slow internet connection. It wants to move the files into Azure Blob Storage once. What should it use?
choices: Azure File Sync, keeping the firm's file server synchronized with an Azure file share
Azure Data Box, copying the files onto a shipped device that Microsoft uploads to Azure
Azure Migrate, discovering and assessing the firm's servers before moving them to Azure
AzCopy, running a scripted copy of the files to the storage account over the network
quiz.explain: Data Box moves very large data sets offline, so the slow network is not the bottleneck. Choice D is tempting because AzCopy copies blobs to storage, but it still transfers everything over the slow internet link.

days.recap: Azure Storage offers Blob, Files, Queue, Table and Disk services in standard or premium accounts, hot, cool, cold and archive tiers with lifecycle rules, LRS through RA-GZRS redundancy, and tools such as AzCopy, Storage Explorer, File Sync, Azure Migrate and Data Box for moving data and workloads.

days.title: Identity in Azure: Microsoft Entra ID, Authentication Methods, External Identities, and Conditional Access

concepts.heading: Microsoft Entra ID
concepts.body: Microsoft Entra ID, formerly Azure Active Directory, is Microsoft's cloud-based identity and access management service. It stores users, groups and applications in a tenant and signs people in to Azure, Microsoft 365 and thousands of other SaaS applications. It also offers device registration and join, identity protection that flags risky sign-ins, and synchronization with an on-premises Active Directory through Microsoft Entra Connect, so employees can keep one identity in both places. For example, a company that already runs Active Directory can sync its users so that the same account opens the Azure portal, Teams and a payroll SaaS app. On the exam, Microsoft Entra ID is the answer whenever a scenario needs a central cloud directory for authentication; never call it Azure AD in your own answers.

concepts.heading: Microsoft Entra Domain Services
concepts.body: Some older applications need traditional domain features such as domain join, Group Policy, LDAP, and Kerberos or NTLM authentication, which Microsoft Entra ID alone does not offer. Microsoft Entra Domain Services provides a managed domain with these features, so you do not deploy, patch or back up domain controllers yourself. Users, groups and passwords flow one way, from Microsoft Entra ID into the managed domain, so you create and change accounts in Microsoft Entra ID, not inside the managed domain. For example, a company moving a legacy line-of-business app onto Azure virtual machines can join those VMs to the managed domain and keep Kerberos sign-in working. The exam signal is a lift-and-shift of a legacy app that needs domain join or LDAP without the overhead of running domain controllers.

concepts.heading: Authentication, SSO, MFA and Passwordless
concepts.body: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do. Single sign-on (SSO) lets a user sign in once with one identity and reach many applications, and when that person leaves, disabling one account removes access everywhere. Multifactor authentication (MFA) requires factors from at least two different categories: something you know (a password or PIN), something you have (a phone or security key) and something you are (a fingerprint or face). Two passwords are still a single factor. Passwordless sign-in removes the password entirely: Windows Hello for Business suits a worker with a dedicated Windows PC, the Microsoft Authenticator app suits phone users, and FIDO2 security keys suit shared terminals where phones are not allowed. Exam questions often ask which methods truly count as MFA.

concepts.heading: External Identities: B2B and External ID
concepts.body: Microsoft Entra External ID is the umbrella for letting people outside your organization use your apps. With B2B collaboration, partners, suppliers or contractors sign in with their own work account or another identity and appear in your tenant as guest users, so you never manage their passwords; you control what they can reach with groups, roles and Conditional Access. For customer-facing apps, External ID can use an external tenant where consumers sign themselves up with an email address or a social account, and the app's sign-in pages can carry your own branding. For example, an engineering firm inviting forty staff from a partner company uses B2B collaboration, while an online shop letting shoppers create accounts in its mobile app uses an external tenant. The deciding clue is partner versus customer.

concepts.heading: Conditional Access
concepts.body: Conditional Access is the policy engine of Microsoft Entra ID. Each sign-in produces signals such as the user or group, location or IP address, device and its compliance state, the application being opened, and the calculated sign-in risk. A policy evaluates those signals, makes a decision, and enforces it: allow access, block access, or allow only after a requirement such as MFA, a compliant device, or a password change. For example, a policy can require MFA only when employees sign in from outside the office network, and block a finance app entirely from unknown countries. This keeps everyday sign-ins smooth while tightening control where risk is higher. When a scenario says require something only under certain conditions, such as location, device or risk, the answer is Conditional Access rather than turning on MFA for everyone.

examPoints: A question that describes a legacy app needing domain join, Group Policy, LDAP or Kerberos on Azure VMs without managing domain controllers is testing Microsoft Entra Domain Services.

A question that contrasts partners signing in with their own work accounts against consumers signing up with email or social accounts is testing B2B collaboration versus an External ID external tenant.
A question that asks to require MFA only from certain locations, devices or risk levels is testing Conditional Access, which turns signals into allow, block or require decisions.

quiz.q: Employees of a small firm sign in to five different SaaS apps with five separate passwords. The firm wants one identity for all apps so that disabling one account removes access everywhere. What capability of Microsoft Entra ID provides this?
choices: Microsoft Entra Domain Services with a managed domain that every SaaS application joins
Single sign-on, where users authenticate once with one Microsoft Entra ID account for many apps
B2B collaboration, which invites every employee into the tenant as a guest user account
Azure role-based access control, which assigns each employee a built-in role on every SaaS app
quiz.explain: Single sign-on lets one Microsoft Entra ID identity reach many applications, so access is removed in one place. Choice A is tempting because it is also an identity service, but Microsoft Entra Domain Services provides a managed domain for legacy domain-joined apps, not sign-in to SaaS applications.

quiz.q: A company wants users to be prompted for MFA only when they sign in from outside the corporate network, and never from inside it. Which feature should it configure?
choices: Passwordless sign-in with Windows Hello for Business on every corporate laptop in the company
Microsoft Entra Domain Services with Group Policy applied to every device in the managed domain
A B2B collaboration policy that treats every employee outside the office as a guest user
A Conditional Access policy that uses location as a signal and requires MFA as the control
quiz.explain: Conditional Access evaluates signals such as location and enforces controls such as requiring MFA only when the condition is met. Choice A is tempting because Windows Hello for Business is a strong sign-in method, but it changes how users authenticate, not when an extra check is required based on location.

days.recap: Microsoft Entra ID is Azure's cloud identity service for SSO, MFA and passwordless sign-in; Entra Domain Services adds a managed domain for legacy apps, External ID covers partners and customers, and Conditional Access decides when extra checks apply.

days.title: Access and Security: Azure RBAC, Zero Trust, Defense in Depth, and Microsoft Defender for Cloud

concepts.heading: Azure RBAC: Roles and Role Assignments
concepts.body: Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC) decides what an identity can do with Azure resources. A role assignment has three parts: a security principal (a user, group, service principal or managed identity), a role definition that lists allowed actions, and a scope. The core built-in roles are Owner (full access including granting access), Contributor (create and manage everything but cannot grant access), Reader (view only) and User Access Administrator (manages access only). There are also many specific roles, such as Virtual Machine Contributor. For example, a contractor who must start, stop and resize VMs in one resource group should get Virtual Machine Contributor on that resource group, not Contributor on the subscription. The exam signal for least privilege is always the narrowest role at the narrowest scope that still does the job.

concepts.heading: Scopes, Inheritance and Azure Roles versus Entra Roles
concepts.body: Azure RBAC scopes form the hierarchy you met on day 4: management group, subscription, resource group and resource. A role assigned at a higher scope is inherited by everything below it, never upward. Permissions add up: if a user is Reader on a subscription and Contributor on one resource group, she can manage resources in that resource group and only read elsewhere. Azure roles manage Azure resources, while Microsoft Entra roles, such as Global Administrator or Helpdesk Administrator, manage the directory itself, such as users and password resets. For example, an Owner of a subscription cannot reset other users' passwords unless she also holds a suitable Microsoft Entra role. Questions that mix up resource management with directory management are checking that you know these are two separate role systems.

concepts.heading: Zero Trust
concepts.body: Zero Trust is a security model built on the idea that no request is trusted just because it comes from inside the corporate network. Microsoft describes three principles. Verify explicitly: authenticate and authorize every request using all available signals, such as identity, location, device health and risk. Use least privilege access: give just enough access, just in time, with risk-based policies. Assume breach: limit the blast radius with segmentation, encrypt end to end, and use analytics to detect threats. For example, a laptop on the office network still has to pass identity and device checks before opening a payroll app, which is verify explicitly, while splitting applications into isolated network segments is assume breach. Exam questions describe one behaviour and ask which principle it represents, so learn the three names and a typical example of each.

concepts.heading: Defense in Depth
concepts.body: Defense in depth protects data with several layers, so if one layer fails, the next one still slows an attacker down. Microsoft's model lists seven layers from the outside in: physical security of datacenters, identity and access, perimeter, network, compute, application, and data. Physical security is Microsoft's job in its datacenters; most other layers are shared or yours depending on the service type. Examples per layer: MFA and Conditional Access for identity, DDoS protection and edge firewalls for the perimeter, network security groups that limit traffic between subnets for the network layer, patched VMs for compute, secure code for the application, and encryption for data. A typical exam item gives you a control and asks which layer it belongs to, so practise placing DDoS protection at the perimeter and subnet traffic rules at the network layer.

concepts.heading: Microsoft Defender for Cloud
concepts.body: Microsoft Defender for Cloud is a cloud security posture management and workload protection service. Its posture features continuously assess resources against security best practices, list recommendations, and summarise the result as a secure score, which rises only when you fix the recommended issues. Foundational posture capabilities come at no additional cost, while threat detection for a workload type needs its Defender plan, such as Defender for Servers or Defender for Storage, which raises security alerts when suspicious activity is detected. Coverage is not limited to Azure: it can protect on-premises servers connected through Azure Arc and resources in other clouds such as AWS and Google Cloud. For example, a team protecting Azure VMs, Arc-connected servers and AWS accounts sees them all in one dashboard. The exam signal is security posture, secure score or threat protection across hybrid and multicloud.

examPoints: A question that asks how to give someone only the access they need is testing Azure RBAC least privilege: pick the narrowest built-in role at the narrowest scope, and remember that assignments inherit downward.

A question that describes a control, such as checking every request, segmenting networks or blocking DDoS attacks, is testing whether you can name the matching Zero Trust principle or defense-in-depth layer.
A question that mentions a secure score, security recommendations or threat alerts across Azure, on-premises and other clouds is testing Microsoft Defender for Cloud.

quiz.q: A user has the Reader role on a subscription and the Contributor role on one resource group in that subscription. What can the user do?
choices: Only read resources everywhere, because Reader at the higher scope overrides the lower assignment
Manage all resources in the whole subscription, because Contributor flows up to the subscription
Manage resources in that resource group and read resources everywhere else in the subscription
Grant other users access to the resource group, because Contributor includes access management
quiz.explain: Azure RBAC permissions are the union of all assignments, and they inherit downward only, so the user manages that resource group and reads the rest. Choice B is tempting because inheritance is involved, but assignments never flow upward from a resource group to its subscription.

quiz.q: A company's security lead wants one place that scores the security posture of its Azure subscriptions, lists hardening recommendations, and also covers servers in its own datacenter through Azure Arc. Which service fits?
choices: Microsoft Defender for Cloud, with its secure score and security recommendations
Azure Advisor, with its cost and performance recommendations for each subscription
Azure Policy, with its compliance dashboard showing denied and audited deployments
Microsoft Entra ID, with its Conditional Access policies applied to each sign-in
quiz.explain: Microsoft Defender for Cloud assesses posture, produces a secure score and recommendations, and extends to Arc-connected and multicloud resources. Choice B is tempting because Azure Advisor shows security recommendations too, but those come from Defender for Cloud; Advisor has no secure score or threat protection of its own.

days.recap: Azure RBAC grants roles at a scope that inherit downward, Zero Trust means verify explicitly, least privilege and assume breach, defense in depth stacks seven layers, and Defender for Cloud scores and protects your security posture across clouds.

days.title: Cost Management: Cost Factors, the Pricing Calculator, Microsoft Cost Management, and Tags

concepts.heading: What Affects Azure Costs
concepts.body: Azure costs depend on what you run, how much you use, and where. Resource type and settings matter: a larger VM size or a Windows license costs more than a smaller Linux VM in the same region. Consumption matters: most services are billed for what you use, and commitments such as reservations lower the rate for steady workloads. Location matters: the same VM can cost a different amount in different regions because local costs vary. Network traffic matters: data going into Azure is often free, while data leaving Azure is billed by billing zone, which is a pricing grouping of regions and has nothing to do with availability zones. Subscription type, such as a free account with allowances, and Azure Marketplace items with third-party charges also change the bill. Resource groups and management groups organise resources but do not change prices.

concepts.heading: The Pricing Calculator
concepts.body: The Azure pricing calculator estimates the cost of services you have not deployed yet. You add products such as an App Service plan, a database and storage, choose a region, tier and options, and the calculator shows an estimated monthly total that you can save, share or export. It lets you compare regions, sizes and redundancy choices side by side before you commit. It provisions nothing and charges nothing, and its total is an estimate, not a quote or a bill. For example, a small company planning to move a web app next quarter can price two regions and two tiers before creating any resource. The exam signal is the word before: planning, estimating or comparing costs of resources that do not exist yet points to the pricing calculator, while reviewing what you already spent points to Cost Management.

concepts.heading: Microsoft Cost Management: Cost Analysis
concepts.body: Microsoft Cost Management is built into the Azure portal and works on real, actual spending. Cost analysis lets you explore costs over time and group or filter them by subscription, resource group, resource, service, location or tag, and it can show a forecast based on the current trend. For example, after a release made the bill jump, an operations lead can group last month's costs by service and resource to find which resources caused the increase. Cost Management also works with Azure Advisor, whose cost recommendations, such as resizing or shutting down underused VMs, help you act on what you find. Remember that deleting a VM can leave its disks and public IP addresses behind, and those keep costing money until removed. Questions about explaining or breaking down past spending point to cost analysis.

concepts.heading: Budgets and Cost Alerts
concepts.body: A budget in Cost Management sets a spending limit for a scope, such as a subscription or resource group, over a period, and fires alerts when actual or forecasted cost reaches thresholds you choose. A forecasted alert warns you before spending passes the budget, based on the current trend. A budget does not stop resources or block spending by itself: it only notifies, unless you connect it to an action group that runs automation. The cost alerts view collects budget alerts, credit alerts for prepayment use, and department spending quota alerts for Enterprise Agreement departments. For example, a team sets a monthly budget on its development subscription with a forecasted alert so it is emailed early in the month when spending trends too high. Exam questions often test the misconception that a budget automatically shuts resources down.

concepts.heading: Tags
concepts.body: Tags are name and value pairs, such as Environment=Prod or CostCenter=Finance, that you attach to resources, resource groups and subscriptions. They are descriptive metadata: they help with cost reporting, operations, automation and classification, but they do not enforce anything, change prices or secure data. Cost analysis can group and filter by tag, so several departments that share one resource group can still see their own costs. Tags are not inherited: a tag on a resource group does not automatically appear on its resources, so to apply it consistently you add it to each resource or use Azure Policy. For example, a nightly script can stop every VM tagged Environment=Dev, even though those VMs sit in many resource groups and subscriptions. The exam signal is reporting or automating across resources when the folder structure does not match how you need to group them.

examPoints: A question that asks for a cost estimate before anything is deployed is testing the pricing calculator; a question about where actual money went is testing cost analysis in Microsoft Cost Management.
A question that expects a budget to stop resources when spending passes a limit is testing the fact that budgets only alert unless an action group runs automation.
A question that needs costs per department or environment across shared resources is testing tags, which are not inherited from resource groups.

quiz.q: A startup wants to compare the monthly cost of running its planned web app in two different Azure regions before creating any resources. What should it use?
choices: Cost analysis in Microsoft Cost Management, grouped by region for the past month
A budget in Microsoft Cost Management with a forecasted alert set for each region
Azure Advisor cost recommendations for the planned web app in both of the regions
The Azure pricing calculator, adding the services and switching between both regions
quiz.explain: The pricing calculator estimates the cost of resources that do not exist yet and lets you compare regions. Choice A is tempting because cost analysis can group by region, but it only shows actual spending on resources that are already deployed.

quiz.q: Finance wants to report Azure costs per department, but resources that belong to several departments sit in the same resource group. What is the simplest approach?
choices: Create a separate management group for each department and move the shared resource group into each
Apply a Department tag to the resources and group cost analysis by that tag
Put a resource lock on each resource with the department name in the lock note
Set a budget on the resource group and split the alert emails by department name
quiz.explain: Tags label individual resources, and cost analysis can group costs by tag even when resources share a resource group. Choice A is tempting because management groups organise subscriptions, but a resource group belongs to exactly one subscription and management groups do not split costs within it.

days.recap: Costs depend on resource type, usage, region, outbound data and subscription type; estimate future costs with the pricing calculator, analyse and budget real spending with Microsoft Cost Management, and use tags to report across resources.

days.title: Governance and Compliance: Microsoft Purview, Azure Policy, and Resource Locks

concepts.heading: Microsoft Purview
concepts.body: Microsoft Purview is a family of data governance, risk and compliance solutions. It has two main solution areas. Risk and compliance solutions, built on Microsoft 365, help protect and manage sensitive information in content such as Teams, OneDrive and Exchange, and help meet regulatory requirements. Unified data governance solutions help you discover, classify and map data across on-premises, multicloud and SaaS sources, so data consumers can find trustworthy datasets, and they show data lineage, meaning where data came from and how it was transformed on its way to a report. For example, a retailer with data in Azure SQL Database, on-premises SQL Server and Amazon S3 can build one map of all of it in Purview. The exam signal is data: discovering, classifying, tracing or protecting data points to Purview, while rules about how Azure resources are configured point to Azure Policy.

concepts.heading: Azure Policy: Definitions and Initiatives
concepts.body: Azure Policy enforces rules about how Azure resources are configured and evaluates whether existing resources comply. A policy definition describes one rule, such as allowed locations, allowed VM sizes or a required tag, and many built-in definitions are ready to use. An initiative, also called a policy set, groups related definitions so you can assign and track them as one compliance goal, such as a set of security rules. You assign a definition or initiative to a scope, such as a management group, subscription or resource group, and it applies to everything below, with exclusions where needed. For example, a European company assigns an allowed locations policy at a management group so no team in any subscription can create resources outside two EU regions. Policy applies to everyone, including Owners, which is the key difference from Azure RBAC.

concepts.heading: Policy Effects and Remediation
concepts.body: Each policy definition has an effect that decides what happens when a resource does not comply. Deny blocks the create or update request, and the caller sees a disallowed by policy error. Audit allows the request but marks the resource noncompliant, which is useful for measuring impact before enforcing. Modify and DeployIfNotExists change or add something, such as adding a missing tag or deploying a monitoring extension. When you assign a new policy, existing resources that break it are reported as noncompliant, not deleted. To fix existing resources for Modify or DeployIfNotExists policies, you run a remediation task. For example, a team first assigns a rule against public blob access with Audit, reviews the compliance dashboard, then switches to Deny. Exam questions test that Azure Policy never deletes resources on its own and that remediation fixes what already exists.

concepts.heading: Resource Locks
concepts.body: A resource lock protects a subscription, resource group or resource from accidental changes, whatever the user's role. A Delete lock, shown as CanNotDelete, lets authorized users read and modify the resource but not delete it. A ReadOnly lock lets users read but not delete or update. Locks are inherited by everything below the scope where you apply them, and they stay until someone with the right permission, such as an Owner, removes them. Even an Owner must remove the lock before deleting or changing what it protects. One Delete lock on a single resource also blocks deleting its whole resource group. Locks apply to the management of the resource, not to the data inside it, so a ReadOnly lock on a database server does not stop the app writing rows. Exam questions ask you to pick Delete versus ReadOnly from the wording.

concepts.heading: Choosing the Right Governance Tool
concepts.body: Three tools sound similar but answer different questions. Azure RBAC answers who can do what: it grants actions to identities at a scope. Azure Policy answers what is allowed to exist and how it must be configured: it applies to every caller and can deny, audit or fix configurations. Resource locks answer whether this resource can be deleted or changed at all right now: they block accidental deletion or modification even by Owners. Microsoft Purview sits beside them and governs the data itself rather than the Azure resources. For example, a company that wants developers to create VMs but only in approved sizes, and wants the production database never deleted, uses RBAC to let developers create VMs, Azure Policy for the allowed sizes, and a Delete lock on the database. Expect questions that list all three as choices.

examPoints: A question that restricts regions, SKUs or required tags for every user, including Owners, is testing Azure Policy, and one about grouping many rules into one compliance goal is testing initiatives.
A question that must allow changes but prevent deletion is testing a Delete (CanNotDelete) lock, while one that must prevent both changes and deletion is testing a ReadOnly lock.
A question about discovering, classifying or tracing the lineage of data across Azure, on-premises and other clouds is testing Microsoft Purview.

quiz.q: Administrators must keep updating the settings of a production storage account, but nobody, including Owners, should be able to delete it by accident. What should be applied?
choices: A Delete (CanNotDelete) resource lock applied directly on the production storage account
A ReadOnly resource lock applied on the resource group that contains the storage account
An Azure Policy assignment with the Audit effect on every storage account in the subscription
The Reader role assigned to all administrators on the resource group of the storage account
quiz.explain: A Delete lock still allows reads and changes but blocks deletion for every user until the lock is removed. Choice B is tempting because it also blocks deletion, but a ReadOnly lock would stop the administrators from updating the settings they need to change.

quiz.q: A company wants every new resource in all of its subscriptions to be created only in two approved regions, and attempts to use other regions must fail. Which service enforces this?
choices: Azure RBAC, by assigning a custom role that lists the two approved regions
Microsoft Purview, by classifying every resource according to its region
Azure Policy, by assigning an allowed locations definition with the Deny effect
Resource locks, by placing a ReadOnly lock on each subscription outside the regions
